newsitem.title: USA: Jefferson Cty, Ky., housing revs A-minus - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Jefferson Cty, Ky., housing revs A-minus - S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, Oct 18 - Standard & Poor's Corp today said it has placed its single-A'-minus rating on Jefferson County, Ky.'s senior lien multifamily housing revenue bonds series 1995 (Big Stone Gap Project) on CreditWatch with negative implications.

This CreditWatch placement is due to poor financial performance resulting from higher-than-expected expenses and apartment vacancy rates. The rating will remain on CreditWatch until the project owner develops and implements a credible plan to remedy operating and financial difficulties. This is expected to occur during the next two to four weeks.

The bonds were issued by Jefferson County, Kentucky on behalf of the Big Stone Gap Corp., a 501(c)(3) not-for-profit corporation whose mission is to provide rental housing for low- and moderate-income persons. Bond proceeds financed the acquisition of Heather House Apartments, a 59-unit apartment project in southeastern Louisville, Ky. The bonds are secured by a mortgage on the project and a senior lien on all project revenues.

The bonds were underwritten to achieve 1.55 times (x) debt service coverage based on gross revenues of $238,500, net operating income of $108,100, and an assumed 7.9% vacancy rate. According to just-released audited financial statements for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1996, gross revenues were 7.8% less than expected, and operating expenses were 24.2% greater-than-expected, resulting in net operating income that was 46.2% less than expected. Debt service coverage was 0.88x.
When the next debt service payment comes due on Nov. 1, 1996, the project owner will make a capital infusion to cover any shortfall. The payment will be made on time and in full.

The underlying causes of the project's poor financial performance are unclear at this time. Standard & Poor's will inspect the project and meet with the owner and manager during the next two weeks to assess the situation, Standard & Poor's said.
